overview.musicalIdentity: Kingston’s pilot history follows the sound-system ecosystem and the evolution from ska through rocksteady into reggae, while treating Rastafari and Nyahbinghi influence as living cultural context rather than decorative genre trivia.

listenHereStatus.reason: Pilot recordings and sound guides are metadata/description-only until playback rights are independently resolved.

gaps: 1 recording references still lack a confident release year

data.name: Kingston sound-system culture
data.summary: Urban sound-system dances provided an important platform for Jamaican popular music and the transition among ska, rocksteady, and reggae.

data.name: Ska
data.summary: A Jamaican popular style that emerged before rocksteady and reggae and became part of the island’s postwar/independence-era musical transformation.

data.name: Rocksteady
data.summary: A slower Jamaican style that emerged around 1966, shifting emphasis toward drums, bass, guitar interplay, vocals, and social commentary.

data.name: Reggae
data.summary: A Jamaican music tradition that emerged in the late 1960s and drew on earlier Jamaican forms, Caribbean and international influences, and Rastafari-linked cultural expression.

data.name: Nyahbinghi drumming influence
data.summary: Rastafari-linked Nyahbinghi drumming is an important influence in roots reggae history.

timeline.title: Sound-system culture as music infrastructure
timeline.summary: Kingston sound-system operators combined amplification, selectors/DJs, records and dance spaces; the culture also helped push operators such as Clement Dodd into local recording and production.

timeline.title: Reggae inscribed by UNESCO
timeline.summary: UNESCO inscribed Reggae music of Jamaica on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2018.

data.name: Nyahbinghi bass drum
data.summary: Smithsonian Folkways describes Nyahbinghi as a three-part Rastafari drum ensemble whose bass drum carries the low heartbeat foundation.

metadata.sound_role: low heartbeat foundation in Nyahbinghi ensemble

data.name: Nyahbinghi funde
data.summary: The funde is one of the three characteristic drums in the Nyahbinghi ensemble documented by Smithsonian Folkways.

listen_for: repeating pulse between bass and repeater roles

data.name: Nyahbinghi repeater / kete
data.summary: The repeater is the improvisatory high-register drum in the three-part Nyahbinghi ensemble documented by Smithsonian Folkways.

listen_for: freer improvisatory patterns above the steady pulse

data.name: Simmer Down
data.summary: The Wailers recorded “Simmer Down” at Studio One, an important early recording in Bob Marley and the Wailers’ Kingston story.

data.name: Studio One
data.summary: Clement “Coxsone” Dodd established Studio One at 13 Brentford Road in Kingston, a major recording base for ska, rocksteady and reggae.
